title: Coffee and cake at a coffee house in Vienna
setting: It's a rainy afternoon in Vienna. You step into a grand old Kaffeehaus with marble tables, newspapers on wooden holders and waiters in black waistcoats. You find a seat by the window.
objectives: Order a Viennese coffee and cake
Understand Austrian words that differ from German in Germany
Ask for the bill and tip the local way
varietyNote: This is Austrian German as heard in Vienna. Standard German is understood everywhere in Austria, but Austrians use their own greetings and many of their own words — "Schlagobers" for whipped cream ("Sahne" in Germany), "Paradeiser" for tomatoes, "Jänner" for January. Regional accents also vary across Austria.

phrases.example: Grüß Gott! Einen Tisch für eine Person, bitte.
phrases.exampleTranslation: Hello! A table for one, please.
phrases.note: The standard polite greeting in Austria and southern Germany. You'll also hear "Servus" between friends.

phrases.translation: A Melange, please (Viennese coffee with steamed milk and milk foam).
phrases.example: Eine Melange und ein Glas Wasser, bitte.
phrases.exampleTranslation: A Melange and a glass of water, please.
phrases.note: Similar to a cappuccino, and the classic Viennese coffee order.

phrases.example: Ein Stück Sachertorte mit Schlag, bitte.
phrases.exampleTranslation: A slice of Sacher cake with whipped cream, please.
phrases.note: Short for "Schlagobers". In Germany you'd say "mit Sahne".
How you tip in Austria: say the total you want to pay (including the tip), or "passt so".

cultureNotes: In a traditional Viennese coffee house you can stay as long as you like with a single coffee — reading, writing or people-watching is part of the culture.
Coffee is traditionally served with a glass of water.
Tipping: round up by around 5–10%. Tell the waiter the total you want to pay as you hand over the money, rather than leaving coins on the table.
The waiter is traditionally addressed as "Herr Ober" — you'll still hear it, and it fits the old-world style.

steps.text: A waiter in a black waistcoat comes over to your table.

steps.speaker: Waiter
steps.text: Grüß Gott! Was darf ich Ihnen bringen?
steps.translation: Good day! What can I bring you?

steps.prompt: First, return his greeting the Austrian way.

options.why: Perfect — the standard polite greeting in Austria.
"Moin" is a greeting from northern Germany. In Vienna it would sound out of place.
"Hello, mate!" is far too casual for a waiter in a traditional coffee house.

steps.prompt: You'd like a classic Viennese milky coffee. What do you order?

options.why: The classic Viennese coffee with steamed milk and foam.

options.text: Einen Kaffee mit viel Sahne, bitte.
options.why: "Sahne" is the German word — Austrians say "Schlag" — and coffee with lots of cream isn't the same drink as a Melange.

options.text: Einen großen Latte zum Mitnehmen, bitte.
options.why: A traditional coffee house is for sitting and staying. A takeaway latte misses the whole point!

steps.speaker: Waiter
steps.text: Sehr gerne. Und dazu vielleicht ein Stück Sachertorte? Mit Schlag?
steps.translation: Certainly. And perhaps a slice of Sacher cake with it? With whipped cream?

options.why: "Schlag" (short for Schlagobers) is the Austrian word for whipped cream — "Sahne" in Germany.

options.text: With a hit of extra espresso
options.why: "Schlag" literally means "hit", but here it's the Austrian word for whipped cream.
A fork is "eine Gabel". "Mit Schlag" is whipped cream.

steps.text: Your coffee arrives on a small silver tray with a glass of water. An hour later, you're still reading the newspaper.

steps.prompt: Is it OK to stay this long after finishing one coffee?

options.text: Yes — lingering is part of Viennese coffee-house culture.
options.why: Right. You're welcome to stay as long as you like with a single coffee.

options.text: No — you must order something every 20 minutes.
options.why: Not in a traditional Kaffeehaus. Staying a long time is completely normal.

options.text: Only if you pay a sitting fee.
options.why: There's no sitting fee. Taking your time is the whole tradition.

steps.prompt: You're ready to pay. How do you ask for the bill?

options.why: Polite and standard: "Excuse me — I'd like to pay, please!"
"The bill, quickly!" sounds rude — especially somewhere people come to take their time.
"I'm leaving now" doesn't ask for the bill — the waiter may think you're about to walk out.

steps.prompt: You were happy with the service. How do you tip?

options.text: Hand over €10 and say "Passt so" — or tell him the total you want to pay, like "Neun fünfzig".
options.why: That's the Austrian way: round up by about 5–10% and say so as you pay.

options.text: Leave coins on the table after he's gone.
options.why: In Austria the tip is usually given directly, by telling the waiter the total as you pay.
Austrian tips are smaller — rounding up by about 5–10% is normal.

steps.speaker: Waiter
steps.text: Vielen Dank! Einen schönen Tag noch!
steps.translation: Thank you very much! Have a nice day!
